# Printing and formatting output

A program that shows nothing is hard to trust. That is why `echo` is usually the first line we
write and the line we reach for most often to inspect a value.

The catch is that `echo` has rules we rarely notice: it adds no separator between arguments, and a
string prints as-is while other values print differently. This chapter covers `echo`, `repr`,
interpolation, and number formatting.

::: {.callout-note}
## What you will be able to do

After this chapter you can print several values in one `echo`, explain how `echo` differs from
`repr`, write `&"..."` interpolation, control the width and precision of numbers, and say why
`echo` and `stdout.write` behave differently around new lines.
:::

## `echo` and its arguments

Save this as `hello.nim`, then run `nim r hello.nim`.

```{.nim}
let name = "Nim"
let year = 2008
let version = 2.2

echo "Hello, ", name
echo name, " was released in ", year
echo "version ", version
echo "a", "b", "c"
```

```{.txt}
Hello, Nim
Nim was released in 2008
version 2.2
abc
```

`echo` takes any number of arguments and prints them in order with no separator. Note the last
line: `"a", "b", "c"` prints as `abc` with no spaces. Every space in the output above comes from a
string we typed ourselves. After all arguments, `echo` adds exactly one new line.

Since every value goes through `$`, `echo` can print almost any type: numbers, `char`, `bool`,
even sequences. A sequence carries an `@` prefix, as in `@[1, 2, 3]`, and that shape makes it easy
to inspect contents while chasing a bug.

## `repr` and `$`

Values print in different shapes depending on the context.

```{.nim}
let text = "Nim"

echo text
echo repr(text)

let score = 42
echo "score: " & $score
```

```{.txt}
Nim
"Nim"
score: 42
```

`echo` uses `$` to turn a value into a string, so `"Nim"` prints as `Nim` with no quotes. `repr`
does the opposite: it shows the machine-readable form. Quotes appear, and special characters such
as a new line show up as `\n`. That is why `repr` helps when values are hard to tell apart on
screen; an empty string shows as `""` rather than blank space with no trace. When joining with `&`,
`$` must be called by hand, because `&` accepts only strings on both sides.

## Interpolation with `&"..."`

Glueing values together with commas gets tiring quickly. `std/strformat` offers a tidier form.

```{.nim}
import std/strformat
import std/strutils

let name = "Nim"
let count = 3
let price = 12.5

echo &"{name} has {count} items"
echo &"total: {float(count) * price}"
echo &"upper: {name.toUpperAscii}"
```

```{.txt}
Nim has 3 items
total: 37.5
upper: NIM
```

An `&` before a string opens interpolation: whatever sits in `{...}` is evaluated and the result
drops in. The content may be an expression, not just a variable name. Without that prefix, braces
stay plain text, so `echo "{name}"` prints `{name}` as-is. Note `float(count) * price`: Nim does
not mix `int` and `float` silently, so the conversion must be written out.

## Number formatting and alignment

The content of `{...}` may carry a format rule after a colon.

```{.nim}
import std/strformat

let name = "Nim"
let count = 3
let ratio = 12.5

echo fmt"[{name:>6}]"
echo fmt"[{name:<6}]"
echo fmt"{count:04d}"
echo fmt"total: {ratio:8.2f}"
```

```{.txt}
[   Nim]
[Nim   ]
0003
total:    12.50
```

`>6` aligns right within a width of 6, `<6` aligns left, and `^6` centers. For numbers, `04d`
pads with zeros up to four digits, while `8.2f` uses width 8 with two digits after the decimal
point. `fmt"..."` is the same as `&"..."`; `fmt` just makes it clear the string is meant for
formatting. A format rule always follows the shape `{expression:rule}`, and the rule may be left
out when the value can simply print as-is.

## `echo` versus `write`

`echo` always ends with a new line. When we want to print without moving to the next line, use
`stdout.write`.

```{.nim}
echo "line 1"
stdout.write "line 2 (no newline)"
stdout.write "\n"
echo "line 3"
```

```{.txt}
line 1
line 2 (no newline)
line 3
```

The last line looks complete because we added `"\n"` ourselves after `write`. Because `write` adds
nothing, we decide when the line breaks. This is the pattern used for a progress indicator that
overwrites itself, or for output that must sit flush against other text.

## When the import is missing

`fmt` and `&"..."` come from `std/strformat`. Without that import, the name `fmt` is unknown. Save
this as `missing_import.nim`:

```{.nim}
echo fmt"{42}"
```

```{.txt}
missing_import.nim(1, 6) Error: undeclared identifier: 'fmt'
```

The message shows column 6, right at the first letter of `fmt`. The compiler found no symbol named
`fmt` in any scope. The fix is one line above the code: `import std/strformat`. The same mistake can
appear for `&"..."`, except the message takes the shape `type mismatch`, because the compiler
mistakes `&` for the plain string concatenation operator. An `undeclared identifier` message always
means the same thing: the name was never introduced to the file, usually through a forgotten
`import`.

## Exercises

1. Print `"total: "` and an integer in one `echo`, with no interpolation, using several arguments.
2. Predict the output:
   ```{.nim}
   echo "a", "b"
   echo "a" & "b"
   ```
3. Write an interpolation that prints `3 + 4` as the sum, not as text.
4. Print the number `7` right-aligned in width 4, using `fmt` and the `:>4` rule.
5. Print `"loading"` without a new line, then print `"..."` on the same line.

Answers are in [Appendix A](../appendix/answers.qmd).

## Summary

- `echo` adds no separator between arguments and closes with a single new line.
- `echo` uses `$`; `repr` shows the machine-readable form, quotes included.
- `&"..."` and `fmt"..."` drop expressions into text and need `import std/strformat`.
- Format rules (`>6`, `04d`, `8.2f`) control width, zero padding, and precision.
- `stdout.write` prints without a new line; add `"\n"` yourself when needed.
